title: Getting Up: The Torque at the Lowest Crouch, the Heat of a Slow Rise, and the Heaviest Robot That Can Stand From the Ground

questions.question: Where in the rise is the knee's torque greatest?
options: At the bottom, with the legs most folded
At the top, where the legs are nearly straight
Half way up, where the body moves fastest
It is the same all the way, since the weight does not change
questions.explanation: The knee's torque is the foot's share of the weight times how far the shank leans from the vertical. That lean is greatest with the legs folded, so the start of the rise is the hard part.

questions.question: The knee's peak torque in the rise for 12 kg was:
options: 20 N m, the motor's peak
2.9 N m, since two knees share each leg's load
5.9 N m
23.5 N m, more than the motor can give
questions.explanation: Up to 5.9 N m rising from a crouch of 0.12 m, against a peak of 20 N m, so a 12 kg robot has room to spare.

questions.question: A rise in 6 s used what share of the thermal life compared with 1 s?
options: A sixth as much, because the torque is lower in a slow rise
Six times as much (0.202 against 0.034)
The same: the heat depends on the height gained, not the time
Thirty six times as much, since heat goes as the square
questions.explanation: In this count the torque at each height is the same however fast the rise is, so the heat is proportional to the time spent: 0.202 against 0.034. A slow rise is the hot one.

questions.question: A 65 kg robot:
options: Could rise in 1 s but not in 6 s
Could rise only from a shallow crouch
Rose, using most of its thermal life
Could not rise at all
questions.explanation: The heaviest body that stays within the knee's peak torque was 40.6 kg. At 65 kg the torque at the bottom is more than the motor has, whatever the time.

questions.question: Why check the rise before trying?
options: Because the plan is needed to choose the gait afterwards
Because the legs cannot be stopped once a rise has begun
A rise that overheats the knees or needs more than the peak wears out the motors for nothing
Because a failed rise always ends in a fall
questions.explanation: The check costs nothing, and a rise that cannot succeed costs heat and wear. So the machine of 36-02 refuses it and goes to a fault and not to another try.

questions.question: What is not covered?
options: The effect of the crouch's depth on the torque
The share of the weight on each of the four feet
The heaviest body that can rise within the heat
Getting up from upside down, and the rise's acceleration
questions.explanation: The count is quasi-static: it leaves out the torque that accelerating the body needs. Getting up from upside down starts with a roll over and is a different routine.
